summary: This informational report captures the results of the second ForCES interoperability test, held on February 24-25, 2011 at the Internet Technology Lab at Zhejiang Gongshang University in China. The first test was reported in RFC 6053, which this report updates with further results.

plainLanguage.summary: Different teams brought their own router-part software to see if it works together. This writes down how it went.

questions: what is a logical function block
what is ce high availability in forces
subtitle: Three independent ForCES implementations swap roles in a February 2011 test and report what worked, what failed and what they learned.

tldr.problem: ForCES separates the control part of a router from its forwarding part, and independent implementations needed to show that they really work together.
tldr.mechanism: Three implementations from China, Japan and Greece were tested on February 24-25, 2011, across four scenarios: LFB operations, TML over IPsec, control element high availability and packet forwarding with OSPF.
tldr.outcome: Nearly all tests succeeded. Two OSPF exchange tests between one pairing failed, which the authors attribute to implementations rather than the protocol. A disagreement on TLV encapsulation was the most contentious issue.

facts.label: Failed tests
facts.value: Tests 16 and 17 (OSPF DD and LSA exchange)

today: RFC 6984 is an Informational report that updates RFC 6053 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It is a record of a 2011 test, not a protocol specification, and the LFB library it tested as a draft was later published as RFC 6956.

sections.title: What the Test Covered
sections.content:
RFC 6984 reports the second interoperability test of Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES), held on February 24-25, 2011 at the Internet Technology Lab at Zhejiang Gongshang University in China. It updates RFC 6053, which reported the first test (July 2008, University of Patras, Greece) and focused on the basic semantics of the protocol and forwarding element model.

In ForCES, Control Elements (CEs) are masters and Forwarding Elements (FEs) are slaves. The test used the protocol (RFC 5810), the FE model (RFC 5812) and the SCTP-based Transport Mapping Layer (RFC 5811), plus then-current drafts of the Logical Function Block (LFB) library and CE high availability, with the LFB library later published as RFC 6956. Three independent implementations took part, and Wireshark and Tcpdump extensions were used to verify what was on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: Grown-ups who build network gear met to check that their separately made parts really fit together, and wrote a report.

sections.title: Participants and Testbed
sections.content:
The participants were Zhejiang Gongshang University with Hangzhou BAUD Networks (ZJSU), NTT Corporation (NTT) and the University of Patras (UoP). ZJSU and NTT were on site in China. The UoP team joined remotely from Greece, and the working group chair monitored remotely from Canada using TeamViewer.

The ZJSU and NTT elements were connected by Ethernet switches, with a SmartBits test machine acting as a router running OSPF and RIP and an ADSL link to the Internet. The UoP elements sat on a LAN in Greece connected over a VPN. Gateways had to allow IPsec, SCTP and the SCTP ports defined in RFC 5811. Sometimes only two of the three implementations could be tested because the third lacked a feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Two teams sat in the same room and one joined by video call from another country. They plugged their machines together and used a special tester that pretended to be other routers.

sections.title: The Four Test Scenarios
sections.content:
Scenario 1, LFB operation. Each implementer acted as both CE and FE, giving six pairings, to verify the protocol's complex data formats such as nested PATH-DATA-TLVs and operations (SET, GET and DEL) on arrays and nested arrays. All 36 listed tests succeeded in every pairing.

Scenario 2, TML with IPsec. The LFB tests were repeated with the TML secured by IPsec, using the Racoon IKE daemon with IKEv2 and ESP. A problem with the UoP system meant only ZJSU and NTT took part, and the four tests succeeded.

Scenario 3, CE high availability. One FE associated with a master CE and a backup CE. When the master was deemed disconnected, the FE promoted the backup, sent a Primary CE Down event and the new master confirmed itself with a SET. This passed. A bug in one FE caused failover to take up to a second because it ignored backup CE messages until the master was gone, so the RFC recommends handling master CE messages first while still receiving backup CE messages when associating.

Scenario 4, packet forwarding. Routers built from one party's CE and another's FE ran OSPF and forwarded packets through the RedirectIn, RedirectOut, IPv4UcastLPM and IPv4NextHop LFBs. Tests 16 and 17, the OSPF database description and LSA exchanges for one pairing, failed. The authors infer an implementation problem, not a protocol problem, and say more OSPF testing is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: They tried four games: asking and changing settings, doing it with a secret tunnel, switching to a spare boss when the first one drops out, and passing real traffic. Almost every game worked, and a couple of bits in the last one did not.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Format Issue
sections.content:
On the first day, every LFB operation involving tables failed. The cause was that implementations used different but legitimate ways of encapsulating data in ForCES messages. For example, a response about a struct can be one FULLDATA-TLV holding all component values, or many parallel and nested PATH-DATA-TLVs, one per component. An array row can likewise be written in several forms.

The testers concluded that a sender is free to choose any structure the IETF ForCES documents define, but a receiver should accept and process any legitimate structure. When free to choose, it is preferred to answer in the same format as the request. For arrays, the formats that put several values in one FULLDATA-TLV proved more efficient, though the nested form also works.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people wrote the same address in two different but allowed ways, and each could not read the other's. The fix is simple: write it however you like, but be able to read every allowed way.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
Developers must take into account the security considerations of the ForCES framework (RFC 3746) and protocol specification (RFC 5810). Because RFC 5811 requires transport-level security by IPsec, the TML with IPsec results in Section 4.2 are the security-relevant part of the tests.

The tests used only simple password security mode, and testing more sophisticated security is left for future study. Further testing with key agility is encouraged: the SCTP TML over an IPsec tunnel established by Racoon included key negotiation, but the authors believe the SCTP TML itself does not include key agility or renegotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: They only tried the basic lock, not the fancier ones, so they suggest trying those next time.
